title: The armor of God (Ephesians 6:10–20)
hookLine: belt of truth, breastplate of righteousness, shoes of peace, shield of faith
tomorrow: how do you see a God nobody can see?

cards: Game day: jersey on, laces double-knotted, the long walk out to the field. People suit up for hard things. At the end of Ephesians, Paul calls himself "an ambassador in bonds," a messenger in chains.

A prisoner may well have had soldiers' gear in view every day. So Paul takes it piece by piece and dresses a whole church in armor that isn't made of metal. And the order he keeps giving isn't attack.

teach.h: WE WRESTLE NOT AGAINST FLESH AND BLOOD.
teach.b: Today's question: who is the real enemy? Paul opens, "be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might." Borrowed strength.
"Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil. For we wrestle not against flesh and blood." The neighbor is not the enemy.
Then the pieces: a belt of truth, the breastplate of righteousness, feet ready with "the gospel of peace," the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation.

teach.h: ONE BLADE: THE WORD OF GOD.
teach.b: Here's one to tell a friend: the only blade in the whole list is "the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God," and the shoes are for carrying peace. And the verb is stand: "having done all, to stand."
Nobody is told to charge. A neighbor tradition says something close, in its own words.
The Buddhist Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation: "If one man conquer in battle a thousand times thousand men, and if another conquer himself, he is the greatest of conquerors."
That's the shared ground: the hardest fight isn't against other people.
And the honest difference: Paul's armor is God's, put on by people who ask for strength from the Lord.
The Dhammapada's victory is over oneself, and Buddhist teaching doesn't center on a creator God who arms you. Two paths, both pointing the battle inward.

how: Some Christians name a piece of the armor of God as they get dressed in the morning, and some children learn the passage piece by piece in Sunday school.

games.q: what does “the armor of god” mean?
o: old metal armor blessed by a priest
a soldier's vow to defend the church
strength from God, worn to stand firm

games.q: the armor, and a neighbor's line — tap the pairs.

s: the armor of God is for fighting people who oppose you
the popular reading. Paul says we wrestle not against flesh and blood.
the only blade in Paul's list is the word of God
the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.
Paul's shoes are for carrying the gospel of peace
odd gear for a soldier: feet ready for peace.

games.q: your little brother says the armor of God means Christians should be ready to go after people. what do Paul's verbs actually say?
o: stand, withstand, and having done all, to stand: hold your ground.
charge: the sword means going on the attack first.
hide: the shield means staying out of sight of trouble.
games.why: the armor is for standing: stand against the wiles of the devil… and having done all, to stand. nobody in the passage is told to charge.

practice: Pick one piece for tomorrow morning: truth, peace or faith. Say its name out loud once, slowly, as if fastening it on like a belt or a shoe. Then sit tall, feet flat on the floor, and simply hold your ground until the bell.

wordCard.voice: The armor of God. Paul's picture of strength borrowed from God, worn for standing firm, not for attacking anyone.

orig.note: Greek: the whole armor, a soldier's full kit, in Ephesians 6:11 and 6:13.

carryVoice: Keep this line: stand, and having done all, to stand, in borrowed strength. Rest easy tonight.
